articles.title: One of AI’s most annoying writing habits has a 2,000-year-old history
articles.summary: “We do not sell products. We build experiences.” If that sounds like a chatbot, there’s a name for it. A new preprint examines why AI models use epanorthosis, a self-correcting figure from classical rhetoric.

articles.title: Why humans punish: A study of two distinct societies reveals a shared sense of justice
articles.summary: Research across two vastly different cultures reveals that our urge to punish rule-breakers balances a dual desire: to compensate victims for their exact losses and to impose extra penalties that deter future harms.

articles.title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage

articles.title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. articles.title: Brain stimulation made people see sexualized women less like objects in a lab test
articles.summary: Is seeing women as objects a fixed feature of perception? A new brain stimulation study suggests it may be more like a habit, one that a mild electrical current can shift, at least in the lab.

articles.title: The science behind the sports betting harm spiral
articles.summary: Frequent sports betting increases gambling harm by making bettors highly competitive and overly confident. When financial losses accumulate, gamblers are more likely to seek professional support if they blame bad luck rather than their own poor judgment.

articles.title: People high in narcissism show less coordinated brain responses to others’ embarrassment
articles.summary: People low in narcissism show closely matched brain activity when watching someone else get harshly criticized. Among people high in grandiose narcissism, a new study finds, those responses are more out of sync.

articles.title: Unpredictable home lives are linked to children’s mental health problems, beyond abuse and neglect
articles.summary: Standard screens for childhood adversity ask about abuse, neglect and household dysfunction. A study of nearly 30,000 children found that also asking about unpredictability at home identified some kids at risk for depression whom the standard screen missed.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

articles.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
articles.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
articles.summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

articles.title: A bad day at work may leave you feeling less in love, study suggests
articles.summary: Work deadlines, family arguments, and car trouble may not stay outside the relationship. A two-week diary study suggests that when outside hassles pile up beyond the usual, feelings of love and passion tend to dip that day.

articles.title: Transgender women show distinct patterns of resting brain activity, small study finds
articles.summary: A small brain imaging study found that transgender women differed from both cisgender men and women in brain networks that handle bodily sensations and movement. On most measures, cisgender men fell between the two other groups.
